ideas.title: Trend-filtered risk parity with a daily trade budget
ideas.pitch: Hold an inverse-volatility portfolio across all 10 ETFs, cutting each asset's weight when it trades below its moving averages and sending the freed weight to Treasuries or cash. Close the gap to target a few percent per day so trades happen every weekday while weekly turnover stays under the cap.

ideas.title: Staggered five-sleeve dual momentum
ideas.pitch: Split the portfolio into five sleeves, one rebalanced on each weekday, each holding the top relative-momentum ETFs that also pass an absolute-momentum filter. Staggering gives trades every day and smooths the timing luck of a single rebalance date.

ideas.title: Turbulence-scaled maximum diversification
ideas.pitch: Hold the long-only maximum-diversification-ratio portfolio and cut exposure to risky assets when the Mahalanobis turbulence of daily returns is unusually high. Turbulence tends to rise before and during stress, so risk is reduced before drawdowns get deep.

ideas.title: Volatility targeting with a drawdown governor
ideas.pitch: Scale an equal-risk-contribution portfolio to a fixed annual volatility, and shrink exposure linearly once the drawdown from the equity peak passes 10%. The governor enforces the 20% drawdown limit directly instead of hoping the volatility target does it.

ideas.title: Ensemble time-series momentum
ideas.pitch: Give each asset a trend score equal to the average sign of its 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12-month returns, and multiply its risk-parity weight by that score. Averaging many lookbacks reduces the risk of overfitting to one horizon and changes positions gradually, which keeps turnover low.

ideas.title: Stock-bond correlation regime switch
ideas.pitch: Estimate the 63-day correlation between US large caps and 7-10y Treasuries; when it is negative, run a balanced risk-parity mix, and when it turns positive, shift duration into TIPS, gold and commodities. This targets the 2022-type failure where bonds stop hedging equities.

ideas.title: Inflation-breakeven tilt from TIPS versus Treasuries
ideas.pitch: Use the relative 3-month return of TIPS over 7-10y Treasuries as a proxy for rising breakeven inflation and tilt toward gold, commodities and TIPS when it is positive. Otherwise tilt toward nominal duration and credit.

ideas.title: Credit-spread risk-on signal
ideas.pitch: Use investment-grade credit's return minus Treasuries' return over 20 and 60 days as a proxy for spread changes, and add equity and REIT exposure only while spreads are tightening. Credit often leads equities at turning points.

ideas.title: Shrinkage growth-optimal portfolio
ideas.pitch: Maximise the expected log growth rate using heavily shrunk mean estimates (time-series momentum) and a Ledoit-Wolf covariance, with a half-Kelly scale and caps on asset classes. It aims directly at the brief's growth objective, while the caps and shrinkage keep the estimates from making the weights unstable.

ideas.title: Hierarchical risk parity with slow drift
ideas.pitch: Build weights by clustering the correlation matrix and splitting risk recursively (HRP), then move toward the new weights at no more than 4% per day. HRP avoids inverting the covariance matrix, so its weights are more stable than mean-variance weights.

ideas.title: Breadth-based defensive switch
ideas.pitch: Count how many of the 10 ETFs trade above their 200-day average; with high breadth, run a growth tilt, and with low breadth, move gradually to Treasuries, TIPS and gold. Breadth is a simple, robust gauge of how widely a market is trending.

ideas.title: Rebalancing-premium equal weight
ideas.pitch: Hold fixed strategic weights and trade drift back toward them each day within a 4% daily budget, harvesting the volatility-pumping gain from rebalancing among assets with low correlation. It is the simplest robust baseline and trades every day by construction.

ideas.title: Online exponentiated-gradient allocation
ideas.pitch: Update weights each day in proportion to exp(eta times the asset's return relative to the portfolio), with an L1 turnover penalty and floors on asset classes. This online-learning rule has regret guarantees against the best fixed rebalanced portfolio in hindsight.

ideas.title: Kalman-filter trend weights
ideas.pitch: Estimate each asset's local drift with a Kalman filter on log prices and tilt risk-parity weights by the ratio of that drift to its uncertainty. The filter adapts faster than moving averages at similar noise.

ideas.title: Three-bucket risk budgets
ideas.pitch: Split risk equally across three buckets, equities (US large, US small, developed ex-US, EM), rates and credit (Treasuries, TIPS, IG credit) and real assets (gold, commodities, REITs), then apply momentum only within each bucket. The structure guarantees diversification across asset classes whatever the signals say.

ideas.title: Absorption-ratio systemic risk overlay
ideas.pitch: Compute the share of return variance explained by the first two principal components; a rising absorption ratio signals that markets are moving together and fragile, so risky weights are reduced. This complements volatility-based signals, which lag.

ideas.title: Short-term reversal tilt within a trend core
ideas.pitch: Hold a trend-following core and use the daily trade budget to buy assets that fell sharply over the last 5 days while their long-term trend is still up. It exploits the short-horizon reversal found in liquid ETFs at no extra turnover.

ideas.title: Downside-deviation risk parity
ideas.pitch: Weight assets by inverse downside semi-deviation instead of total volatility, so upside volatility (common in commodities and gold) is not penalised. The portfolio aligns better with the drawdown constraint than variance-based weights.

ideas.title: CPPI with Treasuries as the floor asset
ideas.pitch: Keep a multiple of the cushion above a trailing 82%-of-peak floor in a diversified risky basket and the rest in 7-10y Treasuries and TIPS. This caps drawdown by construction, apart from gap risk and cases where the safe asset itself falls.

ideas.title: Dispersion-conditioned momentum
ideas.pitch: Scale the strength of relative momentum by cross-sectional return dispersion: when dispersion is high, concentrate in leaders, and when it is low, stay close to risk parity. Momentum pays mainly when assets diverge, so conditioning on dispersion avoids trend-less whipsaw.

top3.title: Trend-filtered risk parity with a daily trade budget
top3.pitch: An inverse-volatility portfolio of all 10 ETFs that cuts assets trending down, targets 8% volatility, has a drawdown governor, and moves toward its target a few percent per day so it trades every weekday within the turnover cap.
top3.mechanism: Each day after the close: estimate each asset's volatility sigma_i with an EWMA of daily returns (halflife 30 days). Raw weight is proportional to 1/sigma_i. Trend multiplier: the fraction of the 50-, 100- and 200-day simple moving averages that the price is above (0, 1/3, 2/3 or 1). Removed weight goes to Treasuries if they are above their 200-day moving average, otherwise to TIPS, or otherwise to cash. Scale the result to 8% annual volatility using a 120-day covariance, with gross exposure capped at 100%. Drawdown governor: once the drawdown from peak exceeds 10%, multiply risky weights by max(0.3, 1-(DD-10%)/8%).
top3.rationale: Risk parity diversifies risk rather than dollars, which the brief's diversification goal needs. A trend filter over several averages avoids most of the long bear markets in each asset. The volatility target and the governor act together as two layers of drawdown control.
assumptions: Trends persist at 2-10 month horizons in these asset classes
Holding cash is allowed when the defensive assets are also in downtrends
failure_modes: Fast crashes (for example March 2020) outrun the 4%/day trade budget
Stocks and bonds falling together (2022) remove the Treasury hedge
Whipsaw around the moving averages in range-bound markets
top3.cheapest_test: A daily-close backtest from 2006 to the present with 5 bp costs, reporting CAGR, maximum drawdown, rolling 5-day turnover and trade days per week, compared with plain inverse-volatility and 60/40 portfolios.
top3.spec: Caps: each ETF 25%; equities (US large, US small, developed ex-US, EM) at most 50%; rates and credit (Treasuries, TIPS, IG credit) at most 50%; real assets (gold, commodities, REITs) at most 40%. Execution: gap g = target - current. Each weekday, trade toward the target with sum|trade| at most 4% of NAV, scaling all trades pro rata, so turnover (sum of absolute weight changes) over any 5 trading days is at most 20%. Trade-day rule: if the week has fewer than 3 trade days by Wednesday, Thursday or Friday, trade at least 0.25% on the largest gap. Data: closing prices only, and signals from close t are executed at close t+1. At least 5 holdings above 3% each.

top3.title: Staggered five-sleeve dual momentum
top3.pitch: Five sleeves of 20% each, one rebalanced on each weekday, each holding inverse-volatility-weighted leaders that pass both relative and absolute momentum filters, which gives daily trades, smooth turnover and diversified trend exposure.
top3.mechanism: The portfolio is five equal sleeves, and sleeve k is rebalanced on weekday k. At rebalance, momentum score = the average of the 21-, 63-, 126- and 252-day total returns. Rank the 10 ETFs and select the top 5, subject to at most 2 equity ETFs and at least 1 non-equity. A selected asset whose 126-day return is below 0 fails the absolute filter, and its slot goes to Treasuries or TIPS (whichever has the higher 63-day return), or to cash if both are negative. Within the sleeve, weights are inverse to 60-day volatility, then scaled so the whole portfolio targets 9% volatility.
top3.rationale: Relative and absolute momentum together have historically captured most equity upside while leaving long bear markets. Staggered sleeves remove the timing luck of a single rebalance date, and they make trading on every weekday a natural part of the design.
assumptions: Cross-asset momentum persists at 1-12 month horizons
Capping how fast sleeves can change does not destroy the edge
Five holdings per sleeve are enough to count as diversified
failure_modes: Too few assets pass the filter, leaving the portfolio concentrated in bonds
The daily cap makes sleeves adapt slowly in 2008-style declines
top3.cheapest_test: A backtest from 2006 to the present with 5 bp costs, comparing staggered sleeves with a single monthly rebalance, reporting CAGR, maximum drawdown, the spread of results across rebalance days, and turnover.
top3.spec: Turnover: on its day, each sleeve may trade at most 4% of total NAV (the sum of absolute weight changes), moving toward its target pro rata, which gives at most 20% of NAV per 5-day week. Trading days: all 5 weekdays, since each sleeve checks its target each week; if a sleeve's gap is below 0.25% it rebalances drift anyway. Portfolio caps: each ETF 25%; equities 50%; real assets (gold, commodities, REITs) 40%. Drawdown: the volatility target plus a governor that halves the risky slots when the drawdown exceeds 12% and restores them once the drawdown is back under 8%. Signals use closes up to t, and orders execute at close t+1. On holidays, the missed sleeve is rebalanced the next day, sharing that day's budget.

top3.title: Turbulence-scaled maximum diversification
top3.pitch: A long-only maximum-diversification portfolio that moves gradually from equities, REITs and commodities into Treasuries, TIPS and gold when the Mahalanobis turbulence index signals stress.
top3.mechanism: The core weights maximise the diversification ratio DR = (w'sigma)/sqrt(w'Sigma w) with long-only weights summing to 1. Sigma is a Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage covariance over 252 days, re-optimised daily. Turbulence d_t = (r_t - mu)' Sigma_3y^-1 (r_t - mu) from daily returns, smoothed over 10 days, with its percentile P measured against a trailing 3-year window. When P > 80, risky weights (equities, REITs, commodities) are multiplied by 0.5, and the freed weight goes to Treasuries, TIPS and gold in proportion to their core weights. When P > 95, the multiplier is 0.3.
top3.rationale: Maximum diversification spreads exposure across factors that are only loosely correlated, which suits a 10-asset set of different asset classes. Turbulence (Kritzman and Li) measures unusual returns and unusual co-movement, and it tends to stay high through stress episodes, so it has some predictive value for drawdowns.
assumptions: Turbulence clusters in time and persists
Gold and Treasuries remain defensive in most stress regimes
The core weights are stable enough when the covariance is shrunk
failure_modes: Stress arrives faster than the 4%/day trade budget can move
Inflationary stress hits bonds as well
The maximum-diversification core concentrates in bonds
top3.cheapest_test: Compute the turbulence percentile from 2006 to the present and check whether P > 80 predicts lower 20-day forward returns for the risky assets, then backtest the full rule set with costs.
top3.effort: Medium: about 3 days, including the optimiser.
top3.spec: Constraints: each ETF between 2% and 25% (the minimum keeps all 10 assets held); equities at most 50%; rates and credit at most 55%; real assets at most 40%. Execution: every weekday, trade toward the target with the sum of absolute weight changes at most 4% of NAV, so turnover over any 5 trading days is at most 20%, and since the daily optimisation rarely leaves a gap below 0.25%, trades occur on at least 3 days. Drawdown backstop: once the drawdown exceeds 12%, multiply risky weights by 0.5 until it recovers to 6%. All inputs are daily closes, and orders execute at close t+1.
